title: An object to remember
hook: Stoics, monks and painters kept a skull or a small object as a reminder
carry: a knot tied in a handkerchief

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ignatius and the last chair. Your line was the last chair. Did you make one choice from there? Today, a way to keep that chair close, sitting on a shelf. Day eight hundred nine.

A desk in an old Dutch painting. A book left open. A candle burned down to a stub. An hourglass with most of the sand at the bottom. A pocket watch. And, sitting calmly among them, a human skull. Painters made whole still lifes like this, and art historians call them vanitas paintings, from the Latin for vanity, the word that echoes through Ecclesiastes: vanity of vanities, all is vanity. They weren't horror pictures. They were reminders, made to hang in a room where someone would see them every day. Today: the small object that does the remembering for you.
screen: `A CANDLE, AN HOURGLASS, A SKULL.` → `A PAINTING THAT REMINDS.` → `AN OBJECT THAT REMEMBERS FOR YOU.`

segments.voice: First, the skull on the desk. In those paintings the objects talk to each other. The candle is burning, the sand is falling, the flowers are about to drop their petals. The skull just says it plainly. The Latin phrase people attach to these pictures is memento mori: remember that you will die. Second, death before your eyes. In the Handbook of the Stoic teacher Epictetus, the advice, in paraphrase, is to keep death and every other thing that seems terrible before your eyes daily, and death most of all. Then, he says, you'll never think a mean thought or crave anything beyond measure. For him, the reminder wasn't gloom. It was a way of keeping desire the right size. Third, a skull in a play. In Shakespeare, the gravedigger hands Hamlet a skull, and Hamlet learns whose it was: the jester he loved as a boy. "Alas, poor Yorick! I knew him, Horatio." The scene turns a bone into a person, and a person into a question. Tradition says some monks kept a skull in their cells for the same reason; others kept a cross, or a few beads. Fourth, any small object will do. None of these things is magic. A skull, a coin, a smooth stone, a dried leaf: each works like a knot tied in a handkerchief. You set it where your eye lands, and it quietly asks the question for you, on the days you'd forget to ask it yourself.
screen: `THE SKULL ON THE DESK.` · `DEATH BEFORE YOUR EYES.` · `ALAS, POOR YORICK.` · `ANY SMALL OBJECT WILL DO.` · then, large: `AN OBJECT TO REMEMBER.`

segments.voice: Look around you, or think of what's in your pocket or on your desk. Choose one small object: a stone, a key, a coin, a leaf, a photograph. It doesn't need to be grim. Hold it, or rest your eyes on it. Let it mean one simple thing: this day is not forever, so let it count. Breathe with it for a while. Then decide where it will live, somewhere you'll see it tomorrow morning without trying. The bell holds the time.
Memento mori, Latin for remember that you will die, the phrase behind the painter's skull and Epictetus's daily reminder. Today's word.
Your line: a knot tied in a handkerchief. Today, each time your eye lands on the object you chose, take one breath and let it remind you that this day counts. Day eight hundred nine.

howItsDone: Some people keep a small object on a desk or in a pocket as a memento mori, a reminder of death that keeps the day in proportion; in some traditions it has been a skull, a cross or prayer beads.

original.note: Latin: remember that you will die. the phrase people attach to vanitas paintings and other reminders of death.

what it means: it's a reminder kept in sight, so the day stays in proportion.
what a scholar hears: vanitas is the Latin for the vanity of Ecclesiastes, and Epictetus taught keeping death in view.
